column2: His sons were great souls, increasers of the Brahman line, ascetics, knowers of Brahman, and founders of gotras.
The blessed Madhuchchhandas and the mighty Devarata, Akshina, Shakunta, Babhru and Kalapatha,
the famed Yajnavalkya, Sthuna of great vows, Uluka, Yamaduta, and the sage Saindhavayana,
the blessed Karnajangha, the great sage Galava, the sage Vajra so called, and Shalankayana,
Lalatya, Narada, and Kurchamukha is remembered, Vadulin, Musala and Rakshogriva,
Anghrika, Naikabhrit, Shilayupa, Sita, Shuchi, Chakraka, Marutantavya, Vatagh na and Ashvalayana,
Shyamayana, Gargya, Jabali, Sushruta, Karishi, Samshrutya, Prapaurava and Tantava,
the great sage Kapila, the sage Tarakayana, likewise Upagahana and the sage Arjunayana,
Margamitri, Hiranyaksha, Jangharin, Babhruvahana, Suti, Vibhuti, Suta and Suranga likewise,
Aradhi, Namaya, Champeya and Ujjayana, Navatantu, Bakanakha, Shyona and Rati,
Shyorucha, Charumatsya, Shirishin, Gardabhi, Ujjayoni, Adapekshin, and the great sage Naradin: all the sons of Vishvamitra were sages, speakers of Brahman.
So Vishvamitra of great austerity was not a kshatriya, O king; Brahman, the highest, was placed in him by Richika, Yudhishthira.
All this has been told to you in truth, bull of the Bharatas, the birth of Vishvamitra of the splendour of moon, sun and fire.
Wherever, best of kings, you have a further doubt, there tell me; I shall cut your doubts.
[Bhishma said:] In the realm of the king of Kashi, a hunter went out of a village, took a poisoned arrow and hunted a deer.
There in a great forest the hunter, greedy for meat, seeing a deer not far away, set his arrow ready.
By that arrow of unstoppable weapon and uncertain aim, a great forest tree was pierced as he tried to kill the deer.
Struck with force by the arrow smeared with sharp poison, the tree gave up fruit and leaves and withered.
In that tree so affected, a parrot who had long lived in its hollows did not leave his home, out of devotion to the forest tree.
Without moving about, without food, weak, with slack voice, the grateful, righteous-souled one withered along with the tree.
Knowing that noble, great-hearted bird of superhuman conduct, equal in pain and pleasure, Pakashasana was astonished.
Then Shakra fell into thought: "How has this bird, in an animal womb, resorted to a non-cruelty that seems impossible?"
Having considered with wisdom this tree, whose life had gone, without strength, its essence gone, its beauty destroyed, shameless, unsteady,
hearing what Shakra said, the righteous-souled parrot sighed very long and spoke in distress:

The gods, lord of Shachi, are not to be transgressed; where you are, there is being; hear that, lord of gods.
mahabharata:13:5.21	I was born in this tree, joined with good qualities, protected in childhood and not harmed by enemies.
mahabharata:13:5.22	Why do you make my compassion fruitless, sinless one, when I am devoted to non-cruelty, a devotee, and a follower?
mahabharata:13:5.23	Compassion of the good is a very great mark of dharma, and compassion always gives joy to the good.
mahabharata:13:5.24	You are asked about doubts of dharma by all the gods; therefore you are established in sovereignty over the gods of gods.
mahabharata:13:5.25	You ought not, thousand-eyed, to make me abandon one able here out of devotion; relying on it, how should I abandon it today?
Delighted by his gentle word, Pakashasana, pleased with his non-cruelty, said to the parrot, knower of dharma:
Choose a boon. Then the parrot chose a boon: the tree's coming back to life, ever intent on non-cruelty.
Knowing his firm wealth of conduct in the parrot, Shakra, pleased, quickly sprinkled the tree with nectar.
Then the tree gained fruit, leaves and lovely branches, and splendour, by the parrot's firm devotion.
And the parrot, by that deed done out of non-cruelty, at the end of his life, great king, reached Shakra's world.
Even so, lord of men, one who relies on a devoted person gains the success of every aim, as the tree did by reaching the parrot.
[Bhishma said:] On this too they recite this ancient Itihasa, the conversation of Vasishtha and Brahma, Yudhishthira.
Long ago the blessed Vasishtha asked the grandfather, "Which is better, divine action or human action?"
Then the lotus-born, god of gods, grandfather, O king, spoke sweet words adorned with meaning and reason:

Nothing is born without a seed, nor fruit without a seed; from seed seed arises, and from seed alone fruit is remembered.
mahabharata:13:6.6	What seed a farmer sows, reaching a field, whether in good or bad, he gets fruit of that kind.
mahabharata:13:6.7	As a field without seed, sown, is fruitless, so fate is not accomplished without human effort.
mahabharata:13:6.8	Human effort is the field, fate is called the seed; from the union of field and seed the crop flourishes.
mahabharata:13:6.9	The doer himself enjoys the fruit of action; this is seen directly in the world, of what is done and not done.
mahabharata:13:6.12	By austerity beauty and good fortune and various jewels are got; everything is got by action, not by fate for one who has not acted.
mahabharata:13:6.13	So too heaven, enjoyment, and whatever goal is wished, all is attained here by action done by human effort.
mahabharata:13:6.14	The luminaries, gods, nagas, yakshas, moon, sun and winds all went from human state to divinity by human effort.
mahabharata:13:6.15	Wealth, a circle of friends, lordship or high family, and Shri are hard to enjoy, likewise, by those who have done no deeds.
mahabharata:13:6.16	A brahmana gains prosperity by purity, a kshatriya by valour, a vaishya by effort, a shudra by service.
mahabharata:13:6.17	Wealth does not serve the non-giver, the impotent, the inactive, one not given to action, the unheroic, nor one without austerity.
mahabharata:13:6.18	He by whom the three worlds were made, the Daityas and all the gods, this blessed Vishnu practises austerity in the ocean.
mahabharata:13:6.19	If there were no fruit of one's own action, everything would be fruitless; the world, relying on fate, would be indifferent, but it is not.
mahabharata:13:6.20	One who, without doing human action, follows fate toils in vain, like a woman who has got an impotent husband.
mahabharata:13:6.21	In the human world there is not such fear in good and bad as in the world of the gods, where fear arises from little.
mahabharata:13:6.22	Human effort once done, fate follows it; fate cannot give anything to anyone without action.
mahabharata:13:6.23	When abodes are seen to be impermanent even among the gods, how will fate stand or establish without action?
mahabharata:13:6.24	Gods in this world do not engage in anyone's affairs; they produce fierce attachment in fear of harm to themselves.
mahabharata:13:6.25	There is always quarrel between sages and gods; by whose word would there be no fate, from which fate proceeds?
mahabharata:13:6.26	And how does it arise, how does fate proceed? So even in the world of the gods many deceits are met.
mahabharata:13:6.27	The self alone is the friend of the self, the self alone the enemy of the self; the self alone is witness of what is done and not done by the self.
mahabharata:13:6.28	Whatever is done or undone is accomplished in the deed done; in a well-done act a bad act does not reach its aim.
mahabharata:13:6.29	The refuge of the gods is merit; everything is obtained by merits; having got a man of meritorious conduct, what will fate do?
mahabharata:13:6.30	Long ago Yayati fell from heaven, was made to fall to earth, and was again raised to heaven by his daughters' sons of meritorious deeds.
mahabharata:13:6.31	Pururavas the royal sage, long ago addressed by the twice-born, famed as Aila, the lord of the earth, reached heaven.
mahabharata:13:6.32	The lord of Kosala, honoured by horse sacrifices and others, Saudasa, became a man-eater by a great sage's curse.
mahabharata:13:6.33	Ashvatthama and Rama, sons of sages, bow-bearers, do not go to the world of heaven by good deeds done here.
mahabharata:13:6.34	Vasu, having sacrificed with hundreds of sacrifices, like a second Vasava, went to the nether world by one false statement.
mahabharata:13:6.35	Bali, son of Virochana, was bound by the gods with the noose of dharma and, by Vishnu's effort, was made to lie in Patala.
mahabharata:13:6.36	Janamejaya, going to the foot of Shakra's sacrifice, having killed twice-born women, what did fate do to prevent it?
mahabharata:13:6.37	Vaishampayana, the brahmana sage, having killed a brahmana through ignorance, and touched by the killing of a child, what did fate prevent?
mahabharata:13:6.38	And the royal sage Nriga, for falsely giving cows to brahmanas at the great sacrifice long ago, became a lizard.
mahabharata:13:6.39	The royal sage Dhundhumara grew old in sacrificial sessions; leaving the gift of joy, he slept at Girivraja.
mahabharata:13:6.40	The kingdom of the Pandavas was taken by the mighty sons of Dhritarashtra and taken back again not by fate but by the strength of their arms.
mahabharata:13:6.41	Do sages, joined with austerity and restraint, of sharp vows, cast curses by the strength of fate, not by action?
mahabharata:13:6.42	One casts off sin in the world, having obtained everything very hard to get; fate does not save the man overcome by greed and delusion.
mahabharata:13:6.43	As fire, fanned by wind, though small becomes great, so fate joined with action grows well.
mahabharata:13:6.44	As a lamp fades from the exhaustion of oil, so fate fades from the exhaustion of action.
mahabharata:13:6.45	Even having got a great flood of wealth, enjoyments or women, a man without action here cannot enjoy; and though wealth is well placed and guarded by gods, the good, by action, rely on it even at loss.
mahabharata:13:6.46	The world of the gods is more distinguished than the world of men; the houses of men are much more prosperous, while those of immortals are seen like a forest of the ancestors; and fate bears no fruit for a world without action.
mahabharata:13:6.47	Fate removes no wrong path and has no lordship; as a done deed goes to the teacher, so fate goes to the chief deed; fate untouched and undiminished is led at will by stored human effort here and there.
mahabharata:13:6.48	All this has been told to you by me, best of sages, always seeing in truth the fruit of human effort.
mahabharata:13:6.49	By rising up, by action begun, by rule and by action, one would gain the path to heaven.
[Bhishma said:] Hear, Yudhishthira, the secret of the sages: by what goal is gained that is long wished in the next life.
With whatever body a man does whatever deed, with that body he enjoys the fruit of it.
In whatever state one does good or bad, in that state he enjoys it, birth after birth.
Deeds done are never lost here by the five senses; they are always his witnesses, and the sixth is the self.
One may give the eye, give the mind, give kind speech, follow and attend: that is a sacrifice with five fees.
One who gives untroubled food to a weary traveller not seen before has great fruit of merit.
For those lying on bare ground there are houses and beds, for the one clad in bark and rags garments and ornaments,
vehicles, seats and carriages for the ascetic, self-yoked; for one lying near the fires, human rulership is said.
One should give foot-water, a seat, a lamp, food and shelter for the honouring of a guest: that is a sacrifice with five fees.
For one who practises hero's posture, hero's bed and hero's station, his worlds are imperishable and go with every desire.
One may gain wealth by giving, authority by silence, enjoyments by austerity, and life by celibacy, lord of men.
Beauty, lordship, health and non-violence are the fruit; for eaters of fruit and roots, kingship; and for eaters of leaves, heaven.
By fasting unto death, kingship and happiness everywhere are said; by truth one gains heaven; by initiation, an excellent family.
Rich in cows by the vegetable initiation, going to heaven by eating grass, a woman who bathes three times and drinks air would gain a sacrifice.
One who lives on water, a twice-born always with fire, purified, kingship for one who undertakes the desert, the vault of heaven for the fasting.
Fasting, initiation and consecration, O king, done for twelve years, is distinguished from hero's station.
Having studied all the Vedas one is freed at once from sorrow; moving in mental dharma one would gain the world of heaven.
The thirst that is hard for the evil-minded to leave, that does not age as one ages, that is the disease ending in death: to one who leaves it, there is happiness.
As among thousands of cows the calf finds its mother, so deeds done before follow the doer.
As flowers and fruits, unurged, do not pass their own season, so a deed done earlier.
As one ages, hair ages, teeth age, eye and ear age, but thirst alone does not age.
By what one pleases the father, by that Prajapati is pleased; by what one pleases the mother, by that earth is honoured; by what one pleases the teacher, by that Brahman is honoured.
All duties are honoured by him by whom these three are honoured; for him by whom these are not honoured, all rites are fruitless.
[Vaishampayana said:] Hearing Bhishma's words, the bulls of the Kurus were astonished and became glad in mind and full of joy.
What is fruitless when applied in a mantra, what is fruitless when Soma is pressed, what is fruitless when poured in the fire, all that is fruitless when said.
This is what was said by the sage; I have told it, lord; in the gaining of the fruit of good and bad, what more do you wish to hear?
[Yudhishthira said:] Even in the highest distress, in what does your mind dwell, in the whole world of men, here and hereafter?
[Bhishma said:] I envy the twice-born, whose wealth is the supreme Brahman, whose conviction is heaven, whose means are austerity and study.
I envy those whose elders and children bear the burden of their fathers and grandfathers and do not sink.
I envy those who are trained in the sciences, self-controlled, sweet-spoken, endowed with learning and conduct, and always knowers of syllables, the good,
whose speeches in assemblies, like flocks of swans, of auspicious form, lovely, with voices like divine thunder-clouds,
rightly pronounced, are heard, Yudhishthira, bringing happiness here and hereafter to the king who listens.
And those who are their listeners, always honoured in the assembly, joined with the qualities of realisation, I envy them too.
And those who, restrained, always give brahmanas well-prepared, pure and good food to satisfy them, Yudhishthira, I envy them too, king.
I should be blessed if I were again even a brahmana, gentle one, born in a family whose course is dharma, whose end is austerity and learning.
No one in this world is dearer to me than you, Pandava; and brahmanas are dearer to me than you, bull of the Bharatas.
As brahmins are dearer to me than you, lifter of the Kurus, by that truth may I go to the worlds where Shantanu is.
Neither my father nor my father's father, nor other kinsmen, were dearer to me than brahmanas.
I know of no wrong of mine toward brahmanas here, small or large, known to the good by their deeds.
By whatever I have done toward brahmanas, in deed, thought or word, scorcher of foes, I am not tormented today.
They call me friend of brahmanas, and I am pleased by that speech; this is held to be the highest of all purifiers.
I see the spotless, pure worlds that brahmanas go to; to them I must go, soon and for long.
As the husband is the refuge and dharma of women in the world, Yudhishthira, he is god, he is the goal and no other, so for a kshatriya are the twice-born.
A hundred-year-old kshatriya and a ten-year-old brahmana are to be known as father and son; of them the brahmana is father.
A woman in the husband's absence takes the brother-in-law as husband; the earth, in lack of a brahmana, takes a kshatriya as husband.
Therefore brahmanas are to be protected like sons, served like teachers, and tended like fire, best of the Kurus.
The straight, the good, truthful, delighting in the good of all beings: one should always attend upon such twice-born, even when angry like venomous snakes.
One should always fear the splendour and the austerity, Yudhishthira; both, splendour and austerity, should be given up.
The effort of both of them is quick: angry ascetic brahmanas, great king, would kill.
More will be given in both if from a brahmana without anger; one should make the remainder from both, and not leave the remainder of what is given.
As a herdsman with staff in hand is always steady among cows, so a kshatriya should protect brahmanas and Brahman.
Protect brahmanas of Brahman's splendour like sons, and look in their homes to see whether there is livelihood here.
[Yudhishthira said:] Tell me this in truth, best of upholders of dharma: the dharma of the wicked men who, having promised, do not give.
[Bhishma said:] He who, having promised, does not give, little or much, all his hopes are destroyed, like the fruit of a childless man.
In the night in which a sinner is born, and the night in which he dies, between these whatever good he did, Bharata, and whatever he offered, all of it is destroyed for him.
On this, people who know the law books say these words; hearing them, best of Bharatas, with highest-applied understanding.
People who know the law books also recite this: he is freed by a thousand dark-eared horses.
On this they recite this ancient Itihasa, the conversation of a jackal and a monkey, Bharata.
They were friends once in the human state, scorcher of foes, and were born into other wombs, a jackal and a monkey.
Then, to the jackal eating corpses in the middle of a cremation ground, the monkey, looking and remembering their former birth, said:
Thus addressed, the jackal replied to the monkey: "Having promised a brahmana, I did not fulfil it.
For that I have fallen into a sinful womb, monkey; therefore, hungry, I eat food of this kind."
This I heard, king, said by a brahmana, a knower of dharma, telling an ancient holy story.
I heard it also further from Krishna, lord of men, Pandava, telling a story to a brahmana before.
Thus brahmanas always instruct me: what has been promised should be given; brahmanas should not be made to hope in vain.
A brahmana, by hope formerly aroused, lord of the earth, is remembered as like a fire well kindled and blazing.
Whom he looks upon in anger, because of hope earlier aroused, he burns, king, like fire consuming dry grass.
And when he is pleased, he welcomes with a word, and becomes like an antidote in his domain, Bharata.
Sons, grandsons, animals, kinsmen, ministers, the city and the country flourish as if by a desired act of peace.
This is seen as the highest splendour of a brahmana here, like the thousand-rayed sun on the surface of the earth.
Therefore, Yudhishthira, what has been promised must be given here, if one wishes to attain a good birth, best of Bharatas.
By a gift to a brahmana certainly the unsurpassed heaven can be attained, especially; for giving is a great act.
From gifts here gods and ancestors live; therefore food should be given to brahmanas by one who knows.
A brahmana is called a great sacred ford, best of Bharatas; at no time should a brahmana go away unhonoured.
[Yudhishthira said:] I wish this explained in truth, grandfather; the course of dharma is subtle, where men are bewildered.
[Bhishma said:] On this I shall tell you, hear, king, as I heard long ago from sages speaking.
Instruction should not be given to a man of low birth; in instruction a great fault is said of the teacher.
Here is an illustration, king; hear it from me, bull of the Bharatas, for ill-spoken words, as before, Yudhishthira, what happened in a Brahman hermitage on the lovely side of the Himalaya.
There was a holy hermitage, with groups of various trees, thick with shrubs and creepers, frequented by deer and birds,
resounding with Siddhas and Charanas, lovely, with flowering groves, crowded with many vow-keepers and adorned with ascetics,
and by greatly fortunate brahmanas shining like the sun, rich in rules and vows, full of ascetics, initiated, bull of the Bharatas, restrained in food and self-possessed,
resounding with the sound of Vedic study, and served by many Valakhilyas and ascetics.
Then a thought of austerity arose in him, bull of the Bharatas; he said to the head of the hermitage, clasping his feet, Bharata:
By your grace, bull of the twice-born, I wish to practise dharma; you ought to tell me, blessed one, and make me a renunciant.
I am of the lowest class, blessed one, a shudra by birth, good one; I wish to do service. Be gracious to me who have come to you.
[The head of the hermitage said:] "A shudra cannot live here relying on the mark; if you wish to stay, be devoted to service."
[Bhishma said:] Thus addressed by the sage, the shudra thought, O king: "What should I do here? My faith in dharma is great. It is understood; so be it; I shall do what pleases me."
Going far from the hermitage, he made a hut, and there, having set up an altar, ground and shrines for the gods, he lived at ease in observance, bull of the Bharatas.
He did ablutions and observances at the shrines of the gods, made offerings and oblations, and worshipped the deity.
Joined with resolve and observance, eating fruit, with senses mastered, always with herbs and fruits at hand,
he honoured guests who came, as was right; thus a very long time passed for him.
Then a sage came to that hermitage by chance, and he duly pleased the sage with a welcome.
Having made pleasant talk, the sage, of great splendour, righteous-souled and of restrained senses, asked him duly.
Thus many times, bull of the Bharatas, that sage went to the shudra's hermitage to see him.
Then the shudra said to that ascetic, bull of the Bharatas: "I will do the rite for the ancestors; show me favour in it."
Very well, said the brahmana to him, bull of the Bharatas; the shudra, being pure, brought the sage water for his feet.
Then he brought kusha grass, forest herbs, a purifier, a seat and a mat of grass.
Then, seeing the mat with its head to the south, wrongly made, the sage said to him:
Make this with its head to the east and be pure, facing north. The shudra did all that the sage said.
As instructed, the wise one did the kusha grass and the rest exactly; the whole rule of offerings to gods and ancestors was told by that ascetic.
The sage in the rite for the ancestors, and the shudra standing on the path of dharma; when the rite for the ancestors was done, he was dismissed and went.
Then after a long time that shudra ascetic, practising austerity in the forest, died, and by that merit was born, great king, in a royal line, of great radiance.
Likewise that sage, dear one, having reached the law of time, was born in a priest's family, a brahmana, bull of the Bharatas.
Thus those two, shudra and sage, were born there, and in order grew up, both skilled in the sciences.
In the Atharva Veda and the Veda the sage became well-established; in the practice of kalpa he was raised and he reached the highest in astrology; and their friendship, too, grew greatly.
When the father had died, he, having done purification, Bharata, the prince, king, was consecrated by his subjects; with the consecrated one the sage was consecrated as priest.
Making him priest, he lived happily, bull of the Bharatas, and ruled the kingdom by dharma, protecting his subjects.
At the "auspicious day" blessings and again and again in rites of dharma, the king, seeing the priest, smiled and laughed; thus he mocked the priest many times, O king.
The priest, noticing the king often smiling and much praised, became angry.
Then in a lonely place the priest, meeting the king, delighted the king with agreeable talk.
Then that priest said to the king, bull of the Bharatas: "I wish for one boon from you, greatly radiant one."
[The king said:] "I would give you a hundred boons, or why only one, best of the twice-born; out of affection and respect there is nothing I would not give you."
[The priest said:] "I wish one boon, if you are pleased, lord of the earth; what you give, great king, say truly, not falsely."
[Bhishma said:] "Very well," the king answered him, Yudhishthira, "if I know, I shall tell; not knowing, I do not speak."
[The priest said:] "At the auspicious day blessings always and again and again at rites of dharma, at peace rites and oblations always, why do you laugh looking at me?
My mind is ashamed at your laughing; by my wish, king, you are adjured; you ought not to speak otherwise.
There must be a reason; your laughter cannot be causeless. My curiosity is very great; tell me in truth."
[The king said:] "Thus told by you, brahmana, even if it should not be told, it must surely be told; listen with one mind, twice-born."
[Marutta said:] "Your family field is mine of my fathers, and I think highly of you; I am not one who has fallen into being unfit to sacrifice for; serve me who serves you."
Vidura and all the others wept greatly, afflicted; and from exceeding sorrow the Pandavas said nothing to the king.
Indra, the Ashvins, the Rudras, Adityas, Vasus and Vishvedevas, and the sages and Siddhas came forward to meet him on his reaching heaven, with the chief gandharvas and apsarases.
Having plunged into the holy river of the gods, the Ganga, praised by sages and purifying, the king gave up his human body.
